headline: Cornell faculty senate votes no confidence in university leadership
author: Susan Svrluga

paragraphs.text: Cornell University’s faculty senate voted no confidence in the school’s central administration in the wake of explosive sexual assault allegations by a former student, according to results announced Friday.
The vote is symbolic — the faculty does not have the power to change the central administration — but sends a weighty message of concern.

“Today’s Faculty Senate vote reflects the deep anger across our campus and sends a clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable,” Cornell University Board Chair Anne Smalling said on behalf of trustees, also signaling the board’s support for university’s president Michael Kotlikoff’s commitment to taking all necessary steps to ensure students are safe on campus, “and working together as a community to help prevent this from happening again.”

Smalling said the board remains confident in Kotlikoff and his administration to “thoughtfully and comprehensively” address the problem of sexual assault on campus because of its track record to date, plans moving forward and the way it navigated complicated problems in recent years, including restoring federal funding and leading the school through the pandemic.

The Ivy League school has been in turmoil all fall, after a former student filed a civil lawsuit against the university, the fraternity at which she alleged she was plied with drugs and alcohol and gang-raped in 2024, and multiple defendants. The university conducted a Title IX investigation and sanctioned multiple students, but no criminal charges were brought. The lawsuit, filed under the pseudonym Jane Doe, sparked a wave of outrage and recriminations about whether university and law enforcement officials had done enough in response to the allegations.

Last month, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) appointed the state’s attorney general, Letitia James (D), as special prosecutor to investigate the allegations. This week, James said that a former federal prosecutor, Jaqueline Kelly, would lead the criminal investigation as outside counsel and report to the attorney general’s office.
A committee of the university’s board of trustees commissioned an independent review to be led by a former deputy U.S. attorney general.

The no-confidence resolution was introduced in October and debated at two meetings before electronic voting commenced Oct. 29. Some faculty senators tried unsuccessfully to delay the vote until after the school shares the results of its independent investigation. And Jane Doe wrote a letter to faculty leaders before the vote took place, saying she felt unsupported by Kotlikoff.

University leaders have taken multiple steps in response to the allegations, including banning the fraternity chapter from campus; launching a task force examining the issue of sexual assault; suspending fraternity parties this year; and signing an agreement with the New York State Police that will enable people to choose whether to have state or campus police serve as the investigatory agency if they want to pursue criminal charges. Cases managed by the state police will be independent from Cornell.

But concerned faculty argued those changes do not go far enough to solve what many have called a systemic problem. Some also said it was important to send a message to Jane Doe and others that faculty supports them.

The resolution, submitted by a faculty senator and with a dozen co-sponsors, states that the faculty senate “has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University.”

Some faculty members criticized the wording as too vague because it does not identify individual leaders, specify failures or suggest solutions. And some called on their colleagues to tackle the problems more directly themselves, rather than solely blaming the administration.

Alexander Thomson, an assistant clinical professor of anesthesiology and pain medicine in the College of Veterinary Medicine, said he is hopeful that the school’s independent investigation will answer some questions that the administration has not been able to publicly answer because of federal student privacy laws. “I‘m interested to know whether university policies were followed, and whether those policies that are currently in place are sufficient to protect survivors of sexual violence and provide adequate justice,” he said.

In this case, Jane Doe ended up dropping out of Cornell, he said, “so there are absolutely things that we could learn from this incident so that future survivors don’t have to face such difficult choices. I think there are improvements that can be made, but we need to be specific about identifying what those are.”
